intro: A car folds against a barrier in a tenth of a second. A satellite falls around Earth for years without ever landing. A magnet slides into a coil of wire and a needle twitches. Sunlight that left a star before you were born lands on your eye tonight. These look like four different worlds, but they run on the same short list of rules, and by the end of this unit you will be able to write those rules down and use them with numbers.

The first half is about motion and force: how to describe where something is and how fast it is going, what changes its motion, and why the safest car is one built to crush. Newton's three laws and the idea of momentum turn out to predict crashes, rockets and orbits with the same equations. Gravity and electricity, which reach across empty space, follow laws that look almost identical, and the idea of a field explains how.

The second half follows energy: the energy of motion, of height, of heat, and the strict law that says the total never changes, along with the equally strict law that says useful energy always spreads out. Then you will meet waves, from sound in a room to light from a galaxy, learn why light is both a wave and a stream of particles, and see how a changing magnetic field lights a city and how a pattern of ones and zeros carries a photo around the world.
bigQuestion: How do a few laws of force, energy and waves let us predict, build and communicate across the whole physical world?

timeline.t: Galileo publishes his studies of falling bodies and argues that motion continues without a push
Newton's Principia states the three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation
Coulomb measures the force between charges and finds an inverse-square law
Cavendish measures the gravitational pull between lead balls, letting Earth be weighed
Faraday induces a current with a changing magnetic field and builds the first generator
Morse's first telegraph message travels from Washington to Baltimore as a coded signal
Joule's paddle-wheel experiments show that work and heat are the same energy in different forms
Maxwell's equations predict electromagnetic waves and identify light as one of them
Hertz produces and detects radio waves in his laboratory, confirming Maxwell
Einstein explains the photoelectric effect with light arriving in packets, the photon
Sputnik 1 becomes the first artificial satellite, orbiting Earth every 96 minutes
Nils Bohlin's three-point seat belt is introduced and shared freely with all carmakers

words.d: speed together with the direction of motion
the rate at which velocity changes, in meters per second each second
the tendency of an object to keep its velocity, whether at rest or moving
the unit of force; one newton makes 1 kilogram accelerate at 1 meter per second squared
mass times velocity; conserved in any collision with no outside force
force multiplied by the time it acts; equal to the change in momentum
a description of the force an object would feel at every point in space around a mass, charge or magnet
the energy an object has because it is moving; one half mass times speed squared
the law that the total energy of a closed system stays the same
a measure of how spread out energy is; it never decreases in an isolated system
the distance from one crest of a wave to the next
a packet of light energy; the particle form of electromagnetic waves

test.q: A car goes from 0 to 20 meters per second in 5 seconds. What is its average acceleration?
test.why: Acceleration is change in velocity divided by time: 20 divided by 5 is 4 meters per second squared.

test.q: On a velocity-time graph, what does the area under the line represent?
test.why: Velocity times time is distance, so the area between the line and the time axis is the distance covered.

test.q: A book rests on a table. Which pair of forces is a Newton's third-law pair?
choices: The table pushing up on the book, and the book pushing down on the table
Gravity pulling the book down, and the table pushing the book up
Gravity on the book, and the book's inertia
The table pushing up, and friction on the book
test.why: Third-law pairs act on two different objects. Gravity and the table's push both act on the book, so they are balanced forces, not a pair.

test.q: A 1,500 kilogram car needs an acceleration of 2 meters per second squared. What net force is required?
A 2 kilogram cart at 6 meters per second hits a 4 kilogram cart at rest and they stick together. Their speed afterward is
test.why: Momentum before is 12 kilogram-meters per second; after, 6 kilograms share it, giving 2 meters per second.

test.q: Why do airbags, seat belts and crumple zones all make crashes safer?
choices: They lengthen the time of the stop, which lowers the force
They reduce the car's momentum before the crash
They add mass to the passenger
They make the car stop faster
test.why: The change in momentum is fixed. Impulse equals force times time, so more time means less force.

test.q: If the distance between two charged objects is tripled, the electric force between them becomes
test.why: Coulomb's law is an inverse-square law: tripling the distance divides the force by 9.

test.q: What keeps a satellite in orbit rather than flying off into space?
choices: Gravity continuously bends its path toward Earth
The absence of gravity in orbit
Air pressure pushing it around Earth
test.why: A satellite is always falling toward Earth, but its sideways speed makes it keep missing. Gravity is doing the bending.

test.q: A 0.5 kilogram ball moves at 4 meters per second. Its kinetic energy is
test.why: One half times 0.5 times 4 squared is 0.25 times 16, which is 4 joules.

test.q: A roller coaster drops from a hill and reaches the bottom slightly slower than energy conservation with no friction would predict. Where is the missing energy?
choices: It became heat and sound in the track, wheels and air
It stayed as potential energy at the top
test.why: Energy is conserved. Friction and air resistance transfer some of it to thermal energy and sound, which spread out.

test.q: Which statement follows from the second law of thermodynamics?
choices: Heat flows on its own from hot to cold, never the reverse
Energy can be created in a hot object
Cold objects hold no thermal energy
All engines can be 100 percent efficient
test.why: The second law says energy spreads out. Heat moving from cold to hot requires work, as in a refrigerator.

test.q: A sound wave travels at 343 meters per second with a wavelength of 0.5 meters. Its frequency is
test.why: Frequency equals speed divided by wavelength: 343 divided by 0.5 is 686 hertz.

test.q: Which type of electromagnetic wave has the most energy per photon?
test.why: Photon energy rises with frequency. Gamma rays have the highest frequency and shortest wavelength.

test.q: Which of these would NOT produce a current in a coil of wire?
choices: Holding a strong magnet perfectly still inside the coil
Pushing a magnet into the coil
Pulling a magnet out of the coil
Spinning the coil between the poles of a magnet
test.why: Induction requires a changing magnetic field. A motionless magnet makes a steady field and no current.

test.q: Why does a digital copy of a song sound the same after being copied many times, while an analog tape copy gets worse?
choices: Digital receivers only need to tell ones from zeros, so small noise is ignored
test.why: Noise below the gap between a one and a zero does not change the bits, and check bits fix errors.

write.prompt: Some people argue that a rigid, heavily built car is safer than one with crumple zones. Make a claim about which design better protects passengers, using evidence from the crash-test story, Newton's second law and the idea of impulse.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence: which design is safer and for whom.
Use evidence with numbers: compare stopping times, and show how force changes when time changes for the same change in momentum.
Explain your reasoning with F = ma and impulse, connecting the physics to what the dummy's sensors measure.
Address the other side: a rigid car does protect its own body from damage; explain why that is not the same as protecting the people inside.
